strengths: Timely and clearly motivated problem: the paper is among the first to systematically study in-generation (red-green) watermarking for autoregressive image generators, a gap the authors convincingly argue via the mismatch between token-level watermarking and VQ-VAE quantization sensitivity.

The core idea is simple, elegant, and well-motivated: clustering codebook embeddings so that all tokens in a cluster share a green/red assignment makes the watermark robust to the token-level instability induced by perturbations. The training-free variant is attractive for practitioners, and the fine-tuned Cluster Classifier provides a natural and effective extension.

Comprehensive empirical support: experiments span three models (LlamaGen GPT-B/GPT-L, RAR-XL), a large perturbation suite (JPEG, blur, noise, salt-and-pepper, color jitter) plus regeneration attacks through multiple autoencoders, with roughly 1.15M images for ablations and 50k-image FID evaluations. The results show large, consistent gains over token-level watermarking and over post-hoc baselines (e.g., near-perfect salt-and-pepper recovery via CC, 14–52% TPR@1%FPR gain).

Thorough and honest ablations: effects of cluster count k, penalty δ, green fraction γ, and the hash prefix κ are all studied, including an insightful analysis of why low cluster counts degrade FID and why some hash prefixes fail (Figure 5 histograms). Runtime analysis (Table 2) demonstrates fast verification relative to diffusion-based regeneration attacks.

Clear writing, a detailed algorithm block, and a related-work section that carefully disentangles the contribution from concurrent efforts (Tong et al., Jovanović et al., Wu et al.), with an explicit discussion of limitations (geometric transforms).
weaknesses: Limited model and task diversity: all experiments use class-conditional ImageNet models at 256–384px resolution. No text-to-image AR models are evaluated, so generalization of the clustering idea to the setting where AR image generation is most impactful remains unverified. The CC also requires per-model fine-tuning (100k images, ~12h GPU), which limits plug-and-play applicability.

Potential evaluation leakage in prefix tuning: the best hash prefix is selected by evaluating TPR across the very perturbation set used for reporting (Table 1 and Figure 3), and Table 7 reports the best-performing prefix per setting. While the authors discuss averaging over prefixes, the main results may overstate deployment performance; a held-out perturbation or prefix-selection protocol would be more rigorous.

The binomial null in verification assumes independent green-token draws, but tokens in an image are strongly correlated (spatially and via the AR context), so p-values and FPR=1% operating points may be miscalibrated; no calibration analysis of the false positive rate on real unwatermarked distributions under perturbation is provided.

Robustness remains weak for the most practically relevant distortions in the training-free variant (blur, salt-and-pepper at high intensity), and geometric transforms (rotation/crop/resize) are not addressed at all, as the authors themselves acknowledge—so the 'robust' claim holds only for the evaluated perturbation family.

Baseline comparability is somewhat asymmetric: post-hoc baselines embed only 32–64 bits while the proposed method uses a token-level signal tuned per model/perturbation set (best δ, γ, k, prefix), and FID-based hyperparameter selection trades quality for detectability in a way that is only briefly justified.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and timely gap: in-generation watermarking for discrete-token autoregressive image models has received far less attention than diffusion-model watermarking, and the paper is among the first (alongside acknowledged concurrent works [13, 28, 33]) to systematically study red-green watermarking in this setting.

The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and practical: clustering the VQ codebook so that all tokens in a cluster share the same green/red assignment makes the watermark signal robust to VQAE re-encoding noise after perturbations. The training-free variant requires no model modification, and the cluster-classifier extension is an intuitive refinement.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: three models (LlamaGen GPT-B/GPT-L, RAR-XL), a wide set of perturbations (JPEG, blur, noise, salt-and-pepper, color jitter) plus regeneration attacks through multiple VAEs and a diffusion-based attack, large-scale FID evaluation (50k images), and detailed ablations over k, delta, gamma, and hash prefixes (Tables 7-9, Figures 3, 4, 7-9). The supplementary material reports full results including variance over prefixes.

The proposed cluster-based watermark (especially with the cluster classifier) substantially outperforms both classic post-hoc watermarks (DWT-DCT, DWT-DCT-SVD, RivaGAN) and the concurrent IndexMark on most perturbations, e.g., near-perfect salt-and-pepper detection (0.996-1.000 AUC) where baselines fail, while verification remains fast (~0.01-0.02s, Table 2).

The writing is clear and honest: limitations such as vulnerability to destructive blur/salt-and-pepper perturbations, inapplicability to geometric transforms, and the raster-order restriction are explicitly acknowledged rather than hidden.
The authors promise public code release and provide detailed reproduction information (generation settings, perturbation parameters, hardware, sample counts), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The hash-prefix tuning procedure (Sec. 3.4, Sec. 4.2) raises a methodological concern: the deployed prefix is selected by evaluating watermark robustness over eight candidate prefixes on the evaluation perturbations. This constitutes a form of selection on the test distribution, and the reported main-table numbers may overstate performance on unseen perturbations or data. While the paper argues the service provider controls the prefix and reports mean/std across prefixes in the supplement, the main results rely on the best-performing prefix, whereas baselines have no analogous tuning advantage.

Novelty is moderate and somewhat diluted by concurrent work: Tong et al. [28] and Jovanovic et al. [13] already explore related token-grouping and token-reconstruction ideas for AR image watermarking. The main delta (k-means clustering of the codebook as a training-free robust grouping) is intuitive but incremental, and the cluster classifier is 'similar in spirit' to prior trained token reconstructors, as the authors themselves state.

The evaluation scope is limited to class-conditional, raster-order AR models on ImageNet (LlamaGen, RAR). It remains unclear whether the approach transfers to text-to-image AR models, parallel/interleaved decoding schemes, or models with different tokenization (e.g., VAR-style), which limits claims of generality for 'AR image generators.'

Robustness gains are not uniform: blur and salt-and-pepper remain highly destructive even with clustering and CC (e.g., TPR ~0.35-0.98 for blur on GPT-B), and the FID degrades noticeably at low cluster counts. The practical operating envelope is therefore narrower than the abstract's 'high robustness' phrasing suggests.

Baseline comparison breadth is limited on the in-generation side: IndexMark is evaluated only on LlamaGen (not RAR-XL), and no direct quantitative head-to-head with the closely-related concurrent clustering method of Wu et al. [33] is provided, making it hard to judge relative standing among token-level AR watermarking methods.

No geometric perturbation experiments (rotation, cropping, resizing) are reported; the conclusion concedes token-based watermarks cannot handle these, but since geometric robustness is a standard stress test for image watermarks, its complete absence weakens the robustness analysis.

The evaluation is restricted to ImageNet class-conditional generation, and image quality is only assessed via FID; no human or perceptual-quality study on the impact of the biasing (delta=5) is provided.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: in-generation watermarking for autoregressive image models, which had not been systematically explored (only concurrent works exist). The core idea — partitioning the VQ codebook at the cluster level rather than the token level so that perturbation-induced token flips stay within the same green/red set — is simple, well-motivated, and clearly explained.

The evaluation is unusually thorough: three AR models (LlamaGen GPT-B/GPT-L, RAR-XL), two perturbation sets of varying strength, regeneration attacks via three different autoencoders, ablations over number of clusters k, penalty δ, green fraction γ, and hash prefix κ, with ~4.7M generated images. The supplementary material (Tables 7–9, Figures 7–8) provides full mean±std results over prefixes, which supports reproducibility and transparency.

The paper is honest about limitations: it explicitly acknowledges that blur and salt-and-pepper noise remain destructive for the training-free variant, that very low cluster counts degrade FID, and that geometric transforms are not handled. This candor increases trust in the reported results.

The cluster classifier (CC) is a sensible, cheap extension (fine-tuning the VAE encoder to predict clusters under perturbation augmentation) that yields substantial gains, e.g., near-perfect salt-and-pepper detection recovering 14–52% TPR@1%FPR over clustering alone, and it beats all post-hoc baselines and the concurrent IndexMark on most perturbations.

Verification is fast (10–25 ms, comparable to DWT-DCT), a practical advantage over diffusion-based inversion watermarks, and the paper commits to releasing code with detailed setup information (hyperparameters, hardware, augmentation schedules).
weaknesses: Hyperparameter selection risks optimistic bias: the hash prefix κ is chosen per (model, method, k, δ, γ) setting by averaging TPR across the same perturbations used in the main evaluation (Table 1 and Table 7 note 'best performing prefix'). This is effectively model selection on the test perturbations and could inflate reported robustness; a held-out selection protocol would be more convincing.

Comparison coverage is limited on the concurrent-work side. The paper relates to Tong et al. (IndexMark), Jovanović et al., and Wu et al., but only empirically compares against IndexMark (on LlamaGen only, since code for RAR is unavailable). Head-to-head numbers against the other two concurrent cluster/reconstruction approaches are missing, so the claim of 'beating the available baselines' is only partially verifiable.

Robustness remains fragile for several realistic perturbations: at strong blur (r=3) on GPT-B, TPR drops to 0.350 (clustering) / 0.691 (CC) while post-hoc RivaGAN achieves 0.996, and salt-and-pepper at p=0.1 is destructive for all token-level variants. The contribution is thus 'robustness under moderate perturbations' rather than a general solution.

Evaluation breadth is narrow in scope: only ImageNet class-conditional AR models at 256–384px. Generalization to text-to-image AR generators (e.g., LlamaGen-based T2I, Emu-style models) and to larger resolutions is untested, limiting immediate practical relevance.

Security analysis is absent beyond standard perturbations: no adaptive attacker, no oracle/paraphrasing-style attacks targeted at the cluster structure (e.g., attacking k-means assignments), and no discussion of the implications of the observed large variance across hash prefixes from an adversary's perspective. The prefix-tuning 'opportunity' the authors describe is a double-edged sword that deserves deeper treatment.

The cluster classifier requires per-model fine-tuning (30 epochs, ~12 hours on an A40) on the model's own unwatermarked outputs; cross-model or cross-codebook transfer of the CC is not studied, so deployment cost scales with every generator.

strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored and timely problem: in-generation watermarking for autoregressive image models, where most prior work has focused on diffusion models.

The core idea—clustering codebook tokens so that green/red assignment is shared by semantically/geometrically similar tokens—is simple, intuitive, and well-motivated by a clear analysis of why naive KGW transfer fails (VQ-VAE encode/decode mismatch amplified by perturbations).

The evaluation is unusually thorough: three models (LlamaGen GPT-B/GPT-L, RAR-XL), extensive perturbation and regeneration attacks, ablations over k, δ, γ, hash prefixes, cluster initialization, geometric transformations (including SyncSeal synchronization), FID and CLIP scores, and verification runtime measurements.

The method offers a training-free variant that already substantially improves robustness, plus optional token/cluster classifiers with adversarial perturbation augmentation that outperform concurrent in-generation AR watermarks (IndexMark, WMAR) and post-hoc baselines, while preserving image quality (FID close to unwatermarked generation) and low verification runtime (~10-25 ms).

The analysis of hash-prefix sensitivity (Figure 5, Section 4.3) is valuable: it identifies false-positive mechanisms from repetitive token bigrams in uniform image regions, an insight useful beyond this work.
Reproducibility is strong: source code is released, and the supplementary material exhaustively documents settings, perturbation sets, sample counts (~5M generated images), and infrastructure.
Security considerations are discussed honestly, including the prefix-tuning key space concern and its mitigation.
Honest reporting of failure modes: geometric transformations are not handled out of the box, and robustness to strong blur/salt-and-pepper noise remains limited.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter selection raises some validity concerns: the best hash prefix κ is selected from only 8 candidates on a validation set, and the main reported configuration (k=64, δ=5, γ=0.25) is chosen as the best robustness-quality trade-off. Although the test set and perturbation set are distinct, the prefix tuning shows the method has notable variance across hashes, and the generalization of the selected prefix is not fully established.

The method's novelty is moderate: it is essentially KGW watermarking with k-means clustering of codebook embeddings, and concurrent works (IndexMark, WMAR, Wu et al.) already investigate token-level watermarking for AR image models, some with similar trained token-reconstruction components. The claimed differentiation (training-free clustering, no decoder fine-tuning) is real but incremental.

The core assumption—that perturbed images decode to tokens within the same cluster—is asserted rather than quantified; a direct measurement of token/cluster reconstruction accuracy under perturbations would strengthen the causal story.

Robustness to Gaussian blur and salt-and-pepper noise remains poor in the training-free variant, and the paper notes these perturbations 'severely limit usefulness,' which partially undercuts claims of broad robustness; the strong results rely on the trained classifier variant.

Evaluation is limited to class-conditional ImageNet models with left-to-right, raster-order decoding; applicability to text-to-image AR models and alternative/parallel decoding schemes is acknowledged but untested.

Table 1 contains some apparent typos/inconsistencies (e.g., '0.8255', '0.9128' TPR values), suggesting minor carelessness in reporting; TrustMark reports N/A for AUC, complicating direct comparison on that metric.

Image quality (FID) degrades measurably with clustering (e.g., GPT-L 4.36→4.85, RAR-XL 3.14→3.96), and dramatically for low k; the trade-off is disclosed but the visual examples (k=8) show clear quality loss.

strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored problem: in-generation watermarking for autoregressive image models, complementing the substantial literature on diffusion-model watermarking. The motivation and problem analysis (VQ-VAE reconstruction mismatch plus perturbations causing token flips that break KGW-style detection) is clearly articulated and empirically validated via the 'No Clustering' baseline.

The proposed clustering idea is simple, sensible, and effective: grouping semantically/geometrically similar codebook tokens so perturbations are more likely to keep tokens within the same green/red set. The training-free variant alone yields large robustness gains (e.g., JPEG TPR@FPR=1% rising from ~0.57–0.69 to ~0.90–0.98), and the token/cluster classifiers further improve results on the hardest perturbations (e.g., near-perfect salt-and-pepper detection).

The evaluation is unusually thorough: three AR models (LlamaGen GPT-B/L, RAR-XL), ~5M generated images, two perturbation sets with a detailed breakdown, regeneration attacks (VAE encode-decode and diffusion-based), geometric transformations with and without a synchronization layer (SyncSeal), FID and CLIP quality checks, runtime comparisons, and a study of cluster initialization variance. The scale and breadth of the experiments substantially exceed what is typical for this area.

The comparison includes concurrent in-generation AR watermarks with available code (IndexMark, WMAR) evaluated at their best settings, and the reported results show consistent outperformance across nearly all perturbations while achieving near-baseline FID and low verification runtime.

The paper is honest about limitations: vulnerability to rotation/cropping (with mitigation via SyncSeal), remaining weakness on strong blur and salt-and-pepper noise, the empirical nature of prefix tuning, and a security discussion of how prefix tuning affects the key space. The prefix-selection procedure is clearly documented (selection on a disjoint validation set and weaker perturbation set A, main results on set B) to avoid test-set selection bias.

Reproducibility appears good: source code is released, model/generation settings, perturbation parameters, classifier training details (100k images, 30 epochs, A40 GPU), and full per-setting results are provided in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: The core contribution is conceptually straightforward: applying k-means clustering over codebook embeddings and hashing on cluster indices is a natural extension of the KGW scheme, and the paper itself acknowledges close relation to concurrent work [39] and to semantic LLM watermarking [26]. The novelty is modest; the value rests mainly on the empirical analysis rather than on a technically deep method.

The hyperparameter search is extensive and the selection of the best hash prefix κ (from 8 candidates) exploits a known statistical weakness of the KGW null hypothesis in this setting: cluster-transition patterns in unwatermarked images (e.g., large uniform white regions) violate the binomial assumption for some prefixes. While the paper documents and analyzes this, the reported numbers benefit from prefix tuning in a way that makes comparison to baselines without an analogous tuning step somewhat favorable; prefix tuning is acknowledged as an empirical patch rather than a principled fix.

Evaluation is limited to class-conditional ImageNet models (LlamaGen, RAR-XL) with left-to-right raster-scan decoding. The paper notes alternative orderings and parallel/masked decoding exist (MaskGIT, VAR, MUSE, HART), and no text-to-image AR model is tested, so generality of the approach beyond this narrow model family remains unverified.

Robustness is evaluated against common perturbations and regeneration, but no adversarial or sophisticated removal attacks (e.g., targeted watermark removal networks, forgery attacks) are considered beyond diffusion regeneration; the security analysis relies on assumptions about keeping the VQ-VAE and classifiers private, which is stated but not stress-tested.

Some results are mixed: robustness to Gaussian blur and salt-and-pepper noise remains poor in the training-free setting, and generation quality degrades noticeably for small cluster counts (FID up to ~19 for k=8 with δ=5 on GPT-B), limiting the robustness-quality operating range. TrustMark reports N/A for several entries without full explanation of why its detection routine could not be evaluated.

Writing has minor issues: duplicated section numbering in the supplementary ((4) appears twice), inconsistent hyperparameter notation (λ vs. γ on Page 6), and the abstract ends with an incomplete code URL sentence. These are presentation flaws rather than substantive problems.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: in-generation watermarking for autoregressive image models is underexplored relative to diffusion models, and the paper clearly identifies why a naive transfer of KGW-style token watermarks fails (VQ-VAE encode/decode mismatch amplifies token discrepancies under perturbations).

Simple, effective, and well-justified core idea: partitioning the vocabulary at the cluster level (via k-means over codebook embeddings) so that perturbed images tend to reconstruct tokens within the same red/green set. The training-free variant already yields large robustness gains while preserving FID.

Very extensive evaluation: three AR models (LlamaGen GPT-B/GPT-L, RAR-XL), a wide range of perturbations and regeneration attacks, geometric transformations with and without a synchronization layer (SyncSeal), ablations over k, δ, γ, hash-prefix analysis (Fig. 5), runtime measurements (Tab. 2), FID/CLIP quality checks, and a security discussion in the supplement.

Fair and informative comparisons: benchmarks against both classical post-hoc watermarks and concurrent in-generation AR watermarks (IndexMark, WMAR) using their official code and best settings, with the proposed method outperforming them on almost all perturbations.

Honest reporting of limitations: the paper openly states vulnerability to rotation/cropping, remaining weakness to blur and salt-and-pepper noise in the training-free variant, and the sensitivity to cluster initialization and hash prefix.
Good reproducibility: source code is promised, generation/hyperparameter settings, compute details, and the full image-generation accounting (~5M images) are documented in the supplement.
weaknesses: Hash-prefix tuning is a fragile workaround rather than a principled fix: selecting the best-performing prefix κ from eight candidates is empirical and somewhat undermines the statistical guarantees of the binomial test; although the authors mitigate selection bias (validation on Set A, testing on Set B) and discuss key-space security in the supplement, the method's dependence on the secret prefix for avoiding false positives is a material weakness of the approach.

Novelty is moderate: k-means clustering of codebook vectors to group similar tokens is a natural and simple extension of semantic LLM watermarks (e.g., Ren et al.), and the trained token/cluster classifiers closely resemble the reconstruction models of IndexMark and WMAR; the contribution is strong on execution but the conceptual delta over concurrent work is limited.

Evaluation breadth is constrained to left-to-right, class-conditional AR models (LlamaGen, RAR-XL); masked/parallel-decoding AR models (MaskGIT, VAR, MAR) are acknowledged but not tested, so generalization to increasingly popular AR variants is unverified.

The training-free variant remains weak against blurring and salt-and-pepper noise, and the strong results on those perturbations rely on the trained classifiers, which somewhat blurs the headline claim that clustering alone solves the robustness problem.

Security analysis is limited to the assumption that the model, VQ-VAE, and classifiers stay private; no removal, forgery, or adaptive attack evaluation beyond regeneration/geometric attacks is performed, and the p-value computation assumes token independence despite correlated token sequences.

Presentation issues: the prefix-selection procedure reads as hyperparameter overfitting risk in the main text, there is a γ/λ notation inconsistency in Section 4.2, and Table 1's dense AUC—TPR formatting is hard to parse; Figure 5's explanation of the false-positive mechanism, while interesting, is confined to a low-cluster regime (k=8) that is not the deployed setting.
